text: There's a worm that eats bone. And it has no way to chew.
When a whale dies and sinks, scavengers strip the flesh in a matter of months. Then the skeleton is left.
That's when Osedax moves in. The female grows branching roots into the bone.
Inside those roots live bacteria that break down the fats locked in the bone — and feed the worm.
It was first found on a whale skeleton almost three kilometres down, in Monterey Bay.
Since then, scientists have found thirty-two species — on the bones of whales, fish, birds, turtles, even land mammals.
So far, that's all about the female. The males are a whole different story.
